content: The United States Public Health Service Commissioned Corps (PHSCC) is a uniformed service of the United States Public Health Service (PHS) and one of the seven uniformed services of the United States. It operates under the direction of the United States Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). The PHSCC is led by the Surgeon General, who holds the rank of Vice Admiral and reports directly to the Assistant Secretary for Health (ASH). The ASH may hold the rank of a four-star Admiral in the PHSCC. Officers of the PHSCC are classified as non-combatants unless directed by the President to serve as part of the armed services. Members of the PHSCC wear uniforms similar to those of the United States Navy, with distinct insignia, and hold ranks equivalent to naval officers. They receive their commissions through the PHSCC's direct commissioning program. The origins of the PHSCC trace back to the establishment of the Marine Hospital Fund, which was reorganized in 1871 as the Marine Hospital Service. Initially tasked with caring for merchant sailors, the service's mission expanded as the nation grew, taking on broader public health roles, including quarantine efforts. Dr. John Maynard Woodworth, a Union Army surgeon, was appointed as the Supervising Surgeon in 1871. He later became the first Supervising Surgeon General, a title that evolved into the Surgeon General of the United States. Dr. Woodworth is credited with formally creating the Commissioned Corps as a uniformed service, organizing the Marine Hospital Service's medical personnel along military lines to ensure mobility and readiness. He also established appointment standards and designed the service's herald, featuring a fouled anchor and caduceus. In 1889, President Grover Cleveland signed legislation that formally established the modern Public Health Service Commissioned Corps. Today, the PHSCC operates under the PHS, the primary division of HHS, and is led by the Surgeon General. The Surgeon General holds the rank of Vice Admiral (O-9) and reports to the ASH, who may hold the rank of Admiral (O-10). Initially open only to physicians, the Corps expanded throughout the 20th century to include other health professionals such as dentists, environmental engineers, pharmacists, nurses, environmental health specialists, scientists, and others. PHSCC officers may be assigned to other uniformed services based on health and medical needs. PHSCC officers wear uniforms identical to those of the U.S. Navy, with unique insignia, and receive equivalent pay and grades. They are commissioned directly into the service, similar to other U.S. uniformed services' direct commissioning programs. Officers may wear various uniforms, including Service Dress Blues, Summer Blues, Summer Khakis, and Summer Whites. In certain duty stations, PHSCC officers may be detailed to other uniformed services, such as the NOAA Corps or the U.S. Coast Guard, where they wear the respective service's uniforms but retain PHSCC insignia. Officers are also subject to the grooming standards of the service to which they are detailed. The PHSCC's mission is to protect, promote, and advance the health and safety of the Nation. Officers are assigned to agencies and programs that provide healthcare to underserved populations, prevent and control diseases, identify and mitigate environmental health hazards, promote healthy lifestyles, improve mental health, ensure the safety and efficacy of drugs and medical devices, and conduct biomedical and health services research. They also collaborate with international agencies on global health issues. Additionally, PHSCC officers are detailed to federal agencies such as the Department of Defense, Department of Justice, State Department, and Homeland Security. Some officers have been deployed to the Middle East in various capacities. The PHSCC has played a significant role in disease prevention and disaster response. For example, officers helped identify and isolate hantavirus in the southwestern U.S., provided clinical services to Haitian and Kosovo refugees, and assisted in relief efforts for natural and man-made disasters. In 1989, officers responded to Hurricane Hugo and the Loma Prieta earthquake. During the 1990s, they provided medical care during floods and assisted in recovery efforts for the Northridge earthquake and the Oklahoma City bombing. After the September 11, 2001 attacks, over 1,000 officers were deployed to New York City to provide medical and mental health services. In 2005, following Hurricane Katrina, officers set up field hospitals and assisted evacuees and responders. The Corps has since focused on long-term public health planning and initiated a transformation to enhance its disaster response capabilities, including a tiered response system with teams ready to deploy within 12, 36, or 72 hours. The PHSCC is led by the Surgeon General and consists of approximately 6,000 officers across various professional categories, including dentists, pharmacists, dietitians, physicians, engineers, scientists, environmental health officers, therapists (e.g., physical, occupational, speech, audiology), health services professionals (e.g., social workers, physician assistants, optometrists, statisticians, computer scientists, dental hygienists, medical records administrators), veterinarians, and nurses. Chiropractors are not currently included, though their inclusion is under discussion.
